Words: Diana Budds

This Brooklyn Café Is Dedicated To The Art Of Matcha

firm: Michael Tower Architecture 
site: Brooklyn, New York

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 2:52
Instaread

Matcha, the electric-green powder mixed into hot or cold beverages, appeals to sight, sound, smell, and taste. It gets scooped into a ceramic chawan, then is vigorously (and audibly) mixed with a bamboo whisk and water or milk to create a frothy, flavorful drink. So when Kettl, a Japanese tea brand, invited Michael Tower to formulate a café dedicated to the leaf, he conceived of a clean-lined yet tactile interior that heightens the senses without overwhelming them. “A direct physical engagement with the environment sets the tone,” the architect says of Sen Mon Ten, the resulting establishment that’s located in the Greenpoint neighborhood of Brooklyn, New York, Kettl’s third U.S. outpost, all by Michael Tower Architecture. “Over the course of the projects, we’ve developed an idea about textures and touch,” he continues, and Sen Mon Ten, Japanese for specialty store, “hits it in a very strong way.”

The 1,000-square-foot spot, previously home to an auto mechanic, is divided into two areas—an open retail counter area and an adjoining, more sequestered room—and an exercise in contrasts. “It’s like an exterior scene inside, to create a threshold for the adjoining private space,” Tower explains of the front portion, which is warm, bright, and where customers can purchase and enjoy their drinks. He painted the original wood-beam ceiling charcoal gray, clad walls in hand-troweled stucco, commissioned a built-in banquette and service counter finished in cement lime, their edges curved for comfort, and selected two rough-hewn limestone blocks for tables—a solution that’s not only beckoning but also seamless in terms of circulation.

The back, which hosts matcha tastings by appointment, is more scenographic, almost spiritual—a setting inspired by Eero Saarinen’s nondenominational MIT chapel. The spare, gray-walled room has a U-shape counter lined with wood-framed stools and capped by a ceiling fixture composed of nested LED-lit white-oak boxes, casting a glow on the host preparing tea. The only color comes from the matcha itself—the star player that every detail in Sen Mon Ten supports.
